title: How the ACLU Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) works: its structure (national office plus autonomous state chapters), its funding (donations, tax-deductible Foundation vs. non-deductible lobbying dues, endowment, attorney's fees), and how it selects cases. They trace its origins to World War I-era anti-war activism (the American Union Against Militarism, the National Civil Liberties Bureau, Roger Baldwin and Crystal Eastman), the Palmer Raids and Espionage/Sedition Acts, and its early and famous cases: the Scopes trial, the Skokie Nazi march, the West Virginia flag-salute case, the Miracle movie censorship case, Smith v. Allwright white primaries, Japanese internment, Communications Decency Act, and the NAMBLA case. They discuss the controversy of defending unpopular speakers, including a Tennessee boy reading his Bible at an after-school program, and the card-carrying member insult. Listener mail describes a fiancée converted to the show.

entities.name: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

segments.title: Opening banter and ACLU controversy
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the ACLU's controversial reputation, the Onion headline about the clan, and a Tennessee after-school program case where a boy was reading his Bible; they say the ACLU defends expression regardless of popularity.

segments.title: What the ACLU does and why it is polarizing
segments.summary: The ACLU handles about six thousand court cases a year, has around half a million members and about two hundred staff attorneys, and is organized into a national group plus state chapters that sometimes disagree. Its policy of defending everyone, including Nazis and clansmen, makes it unpopular.

segments.title: WWI-era anti-war activists and the Palmer Raids
segments.summary: The ACLU's roots lie in World War I anti-war groups such as the American Union Against Militarism. Under the Espionage Act and Sedition Act of 1918, anti-war speakers faced long prison terms, and the Palmer Raids rounded up suspected radicals without warrants or due process.

segments.title: Founding of the ACLU from the National Civil Liberties Bureau
segments.summary: Crystal Eastman and Roger Baldwin started legal assistance for jailed activists through the Civil Liberties Bureau, which later became the National Civil Liberties Bureau and then the American Civil Liberties Union, born January 19, 1920. Courts of the era were hostile to free speech claims.

segments.title: Early cases: Scopes trial and Skokie
segments.summary: In the 1920s and 1930s the ACLU began winning smaller cases. It backed John Scopes in the Tennessee evolution-teaching case, which it lost (the verdict was later overturned on a sentencing error). The hosts also discuss the ACLU defending the Ku Klux Klan's rights while defending Black civil rights groups, and the 1977-78 Skokie Nazi march controversy, where the Nazis never held their march.

segments.title: Landmark cases: flag salute, The Miracle, white primaries
segments.summary: The ACLU helped win West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, protecting Jehovah's Witness students who refused the Pledge of Allegiance; the case concerning the film The Miracle, which the Supreme Court said the state had no legitimate interest in protecting religions from distasteful views; and Smith v. Allwright, which struck down white primaries.

segments.title: More landmark cases and the NAMBLA controversy
segments.summary: The hosts list further famous cases the ACLU was involved in, including Japanese internment, Brown v. Board of Education, Roe v. Wade, and the Communications Decency Act. They discuss the ACLU's defense of NAMBLA, which was found to be an unincorporated association whose speech was protected, and the suit against it was dismissed.

segments.title: How to get ACLU help, funding, and the card-carrying member insult
segments.summary: Cases are submitted by letter and the ACLU often resolves issues by writing to agencies before litigating. Funding comes from donations, a tax-deductible foundation that litigates, a non-deductible lobbying arm funded by dues, an endowment, and attorney's fees, which critics say can intimidate towns. The phrase 'card carrying member' came from Michael du Bois and was used by George H. W. Bush.

segments.title: Listener mail: converting a fiancée
segments.summary: A listener from Horsham, England, describes converting his fiancée Kathy to the show, starting with the JFK episode and succeeding with the Malaysia Flight 370 black box episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts encourage listeners to connect on social media and send email, and sign off.
